Following in Vision-Language-Action Models
Sangwu Park Wonjoong Kim Yeonjun In Chanyoung Park *
KAIST
{sangwu.park, wjkim, yeonjun.in, cy.park}@kaist.ac.kr
Abstract
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are ex-
pected to follow instructions like their language
backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-
level instructions that specify the task rather
than How-level instructions that specify how to
carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find
that How-level instructions do not help current
VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize
that pairing each training episode with a single
instruction limits How-level instruction follow-
ing, and show that training with segment-level
enriched instructions makes actions respond to
such instructions without consistently raising
task success. To measure How-level instruc-
tion following beyond standard benchmarks,
we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success re-
quires conditions given only in the instruction.
It shows that the gained responsiveness does
not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution
How-level instructions. How-level instruction
following thus remains an open challenge.1
1 Introduction
Completing a task specified by a language instruc-
tion does not necessarily mean following instruc-
tions on how to perform it. For example, “put the
carrot on the plate” specifieswhata robot should
accomplish, whereas “grasp the carrot by its green
end” specifieshowto accomplish it. This distinc-
tion is particularly important for vision-language-
action (VLA) models, which generate robot ac-
tions from visual observations and language in-
structions (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024;
Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck
et al., 2025). Following instructions abouthow
to act would enable VLAs to incorporate correc-
tions, refine actions, and adjust their behavior
through language, as widely practiced in large lan-
guage models (LLMs) and vision-language models
